name: Carla Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a commis, the lowest rank of cook, at Lumen, an all-day restaurant in an old tram depot. I start at six for brunch: hollandaise, pancake batter, forty portions of shakshuka base. Then I help the pastry chef, Hana, with the afternoon tarts, and I'm out by four unless someone calls in sick. Weekends we do about three hundred covers across the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the pastry side, because it's precise and I'm a bit of a nerd. I'm still messy though, my piping is awful and Hana redoes about half of it. What wears me out is the six o'clock starts and the brunch tickets that all come in at eleven at once. I use AI every day to learn techniques and plan my Sunday supper club, which keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, okay. I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the hype was always bigger than the tools. Online I'd probably post something about how the chatbot still can't tell me why my choux pastry collapses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it means my life stays good. I've got about ten months of costs saved, I sold my dad's old car last year, and Ines, my girlfriend, has steady design clients. If AI stays a toy, I stay a junior who's bad at piping, with a good savings account and a supper club on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Lumen and keep using the AI tools I already use, for costing my supper club menus and practising French pastry terms. I'd grow the supper club from one Sunday a month to two this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little flat, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the supper club.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's twelve people around our kitchen table, set menu, they pay thirty-five each. I plan it with AI, it does the shopping list and the costs, and I cook. It's where I'm not the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent going up, maybe, and the early shifts. But nothing big. My cushion is decent for someone my age.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always bigger than the tools.
I'd joke online that the chatbot can't fix my **choux pastry**.
think: My **savings** and Ines's design clients make life stable.
Nothing changes for me except I stay a **junior**.
do: Keep using AI for **supper club costing** and pastry study.
Grow the **supper club** from one Sunday a month to two.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly **flat** because she likes new things.
S0.quote: If AI stays a toy, I stay a junior who's bad at piping, with a good savings account and a supper club on Sundays.
fieldNote: She is an **everyday AI user** and finds a plateau a little dull.
Her **supper club** is where she gets status she lacks at work.
Her household relies on **Ines's design work**, which matters later.

steps.text: Keep cooking brunch and pastry at Lumen
Run the supper club twice a month instead of once

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, planning, booking. That's Ines's world more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper safety net for people whose work gets taken, things like retraining paid by the state. And I'd say AI is great for small people like me, if it's shared fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried about Ines first. She does logos and menus for small businesses, and those clients would start making their own with AI. The robots aren't coming for my kitchen yet, but AI could take half the logo work my girlfriend Ines does by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the supper club harder, because people pay for a human cooking in front of them. I'd help Ines move into something hands-on, maybe she does signage painting, she's always wanted to. And I'd use AI even more to plan, because it's a tool that saves me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. It's more about us than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your household money if Ines's clients drop off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We split rent fifty-fifty, eleven hundred each. If she loses half her clients, I'd cover more and we'd dip into my savings. We'd manage for a year, maybe two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI is great for small people. Isn't that what's hurting Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. It's both, and I can't make it tidy. I'd still use it, I'd just be angrier about who gets the money from it.

say: I'd call for **state-paid retraining** for people whose work goes.
I'd say AI helps **small people**, if the gains are shared.
think: **Ines's design work** is at risk before my cooking is.
Our **fifty-fifty rent** could fall on me.
My own kitchen job feels **safe for now**.
do: Grow the **supper club** because people pay for human cooking.
Help Ines try **signage painting** as hands-on work.
Use AI more to **save hours** on planning.
S1.quote: The robots aren't coming for my kitchen yet, but AI could take half the logo work my girlfriend Ines does by next year.
fieldNote: Her worry centres on her **partner's income**, not her own job.
She holds a **contradiction**: AI helps her, hurts Ines.
She sees **live human cooking** as something people will pay more for.

steps.text: Advertise the supper club as live human cooking
Help Ines start taking signage painting jobs
Use AI to cut supper club planning time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. 2028, so AI is here before Ines can turn around, and kitchen robots by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, money everyone gets, paid for by the companies who own the AI. I'd be at the marches and I'd post every day. This can't just be left to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be hit twice. Ines loses most of her work in 2028, and then my job at Lumen goes when the kitchen robots arrive. Being good with AI only helps me if there's still a job left once AI is doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back, no holidays, and keep my savings as cash. I'd try to build the supper club into a real small business before 2031, maybe a licensed space with my name on it. And I'd go deep into AI tools to run the business side, so I can spend my time on the cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines say to each other that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're lucky to have savings, and that it won't last two incomes falling. Maybe we'd talk about moving somewhere cheaper. Ines would cry, she cries when she's scared, and I'd make pancakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're adaptive, you like new tech. Doesn't that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me move fast, yes. But knowing how to use AI doesn't pay the rent when AI is doing the job. Being early only helps if there's still a job to be early to.

I'd say this **can't be left** to the market.
think: We'd be **hit twice**: Ines in 2028, me in 2031.
Our **savings** won't survive both incomes falling.

feel: **Alarmed**, doing sums at three in the **morning**.
S2.quote: Being good with AI only helps me if there's still a job left once AI is doing it.
fieldNote: She expects **both household incomes** to fall within three years.
She sees the limit of being **tech-savvy** when jobs vanish.
Her plan is to **own** something, not just work for someone.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and keep savings in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, five years. Ines gets a bit of time, and I'd be thirty-five when robots reach kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same about basic income, but I'd also say this is when communities should build things together. Shared kitchens, co-ops, places where people still cook and eat together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd be okay if we used the time. Five years is enough time to turn a supper club around my kitchen table into a real co-op kitchen with friends. Ines could retrain, and I'd build the supper club slowly into a small co-op kitchen with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, start saving towards a shared kitchen with two friends from other restaurants. Help Ines start a sign-painting course at night. Keep at Lumen and get better at pastry, because by 2034 I want to be good enough to sell my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. The good kind, if there is one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the friends you'd start with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás, who's a line cook at a burger place, and Wren, who bakes bread at night. We've talked about it as a dream. Five years would turn it into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in 2031, when the AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use it for everything that isn't cooking, the bookings, the accounts, the orders. That frees us to just cook, which is the bit robots won't be doing until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse not to get this right: shorter working weeks, basic income, free retraining. I'd vote for whoever promised it and keep posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd come out of this one fine. Ten years is long enough for me to go from bad at piping to running my own little restaurant, with AI doing the paperwork. By 2039 I'd want my own small place, using AI for everything except the food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train properly at Lumen for three or four years, maybe move up to pastry chef. Keep the supper club as practice for running a business. Start a small business course in about 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for other people more than for me. Excited, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older cooks at Lumen. Our dishwasher, Hector, is fifty-eight and has done this for thirty years. Ten years is good for me but not for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be fine with ten years. She's talented, she'd have time to move into painting signs or murals. We might even buy a place by then.

I'd vote for **shorter weeks** and free retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us get hit, Ines first and then me. Everyone asks if the robots will take my kitchen job, but my girlfriend's design work is the job in our flat that AI takes first. What would help is a basic income, or at least real money to start small businesses, so people like us can build something instead of just waiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who's in the household, not just who's in the job. My kitchen job is the safe one in our flat, and that surprised me.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots will take my kitchen job, but my girlfriend's design work is the job in our flat that AI takes first.
portrait: Carla is a **junior commis** at Lumen, a busy all-day restaurant, and loves pastry.
She has **ten months saved** and runs a monthly supper club.
She uses **AI daily** and backs a basic income and co-ops.
Her worry centres on **Ines**, her girlfriend, whose design work AI reaches first.
She's **calm** if AI stalls and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Ines loses work first and Carla's **job** follows.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or real **start-up money** for small businesses.
